chapter_theme: The first twenty-five units of Pattinathar's Mummanikkovai on Thiruvidaimaruthur: long agavals that praise Siva's half-woman form limb by limb, dissect the poet's own body and find no 'I' in it, farm the field of the heart until the five-letter fruit ripens, and set the lives of the householder, the self-tormenting ascetic and the devotee side by side, interleaved with short venbas and kalitthurais that tell the heart to say the name, hold the devotees' feet and give up women. Pattinathar's claim throughout is that birth is a prison and grace the only way out of it, and that grace answers a green leaf, a word or a thought as well as any austerity.
structure_note: A மும்மணிக்கோவை rotates three metres, ஆசிரியப்பா, வெண்பா and கட்டளைக்கலித்துறை, in that order (812, 813, 814; 815, 816, 817 and so on), and each unit begins with the last word of the one before (திருவடி / பொருள், வரும் / வருந்தேன், கதி / கதியாவது). The metre labels printed beside the ids accumulate the previous unit's metre and are not reliable for the unit they stand beside. 822, 834 (and 850, 852 in the Kazhumalam kovai) are akam fragments in a woman's voice, the kovai's love element.

812.reading: The poet praises the Lord of Marudur limb by limb in two halves: one foot red as a divine lotus that kicked Death and that Vishnu as a boar could not dig to, the other a soft karpaka shoot that even anklets hurt; one waist in tiger skin belted with a snake, the other in red cloth with a jewelled girdle; one chest with snake, tortoise, boar tusk, rudraksha and white ash like a coral hill, the other with breasts that bore seven worlds; one hand with trident, axe and drum, the other with bangles, a ball and a parrot; one eye hot with sun and fire, the other cool as a lily pitying our confusion; one crown with nochi, datura, konrai, Ganga, skull, snake and moon on fire-red matted hair beyond Brahma's swan, the other blue hair in a garland of karpaka flowers; two forms in one body, the right eye and the left glance, the right hand caressing the left breast so that the hair rises: we praise the feet of this one God of Marudur who gives release even to devotees who offer a green leaf, so that, having died and been born and grown weary for long days, we may not enter the prison of the womb again but gain a life that does not return.
812.nuance: The whole description is organised by ஒருபால் (one side) to show the half-woman form, and the kovai's akam voice later treats Ganga and Uma as rivals (834). பத்தி அடியவர் பச்சிலை இடினும் முத்தி கொடுத்து, release for a green leaf, is the claim the work returns to (825, 830, 833, 853). சிறைக் கருப்பாசயம், the prison of the womb, is developed at 833.

813.reading: Wealth, lineage, fame, ability, grace and knowledge, all of it, come to those who say 'dark-throated one, ancient Lord of Marudur', even to those who say they want none of it.
813.nuance: ஒருவர் கருதா என்பார்க்கும் is compressed: it may mean these things come even to those who do not seek them, or that they come to those who hold no one else in mind. Either way the name alone is the condition.

814.reading: I will not grieve, dying and being born along the way of the deluding senses; I will not join that way and so do not enter birth; having scooped and eaten the great honey of famous Marudur, I stayed with no desire for anything else, and now I will not go and beg anything from anyone.
814.nuance: பெருந்தேன் முகந்து உண்டு, scooping and eating the great honey, is the poet's figure for the taste of the Lord that ends wanting; the venba before promised everything to those who say the name, and this verse answers that there is nothing left to want. இரவேன் ஒருவரை, I will not beg from anyone, is the Kural's language of இரவு turned to the mendicant poet's one refusal.

815.reading: After praising Marudur, its cloud-touching mansions, streets and women, and its Lord with the axe, the Lord the Vedas cannot follow, the full and ancient one, the cause-God Vishnu does not know, the single light, lord of the one and of yoga, the poet says he has one thing to tell: born in endless wombs in the endless world and spun like a whirling top, he knows the pain at birth, the pain the mother suffers and he suffers, and the pain at death, and who knows them but you; so he cannot bear birth again, and there is no way to wipe out birth except holding you; that way needs a mind that leans to neither wanting nor loathing, but his mind stands at the command of the five senses and takes another thing for itself, so how is he to think of you with it; who has ever swum the sea on a raft of stone; Lord, he must gain the crossing of the aeon, and the thought for crossing, and a heart that stands on the way for thinking, O one with the venom-fanged serpent, the dark throat and the eye in the forehead.
815.nuance: கற்புணை ஆகக் கடல்நீர் நீந்தினர் எற்பிறர் உளரோ, who else has swum the sea on a stone float, is the image for trying to cross birth with a sense-driven mind. கற்பங் கடத்தல் is read here as crossing the aeon, that is, outlasting the kalpa; it could also be crossing to the far shore in general. The three wants at the end (the crossing, the thought, the steady heart) are asked of the Lord, not of practice.

816.reading: Calling you our eye, our protection, the number we have learned and the root letter, O bright Lord of Marudur, if we do not praise you, is there any refuge beyond for thought to find?
816.nuance: கற்றிருக்கும் எண் and மூல எழுத்து treat the Lord as the thing counted and the root syllable of the mantra, so praising him is also reciting it. கதி (refuge, goal) is picked up as the first word of 817.

817.reading: There is no other goal; if you carry the bundle that is this body it will fall and go, and after it has gone some grieve and call it fate; who wants this; wisdom is to go and praise the anklet feet of the Lord of Marudur.
817.nuance: களேபரத்தின் பொதி, the bundle of the carcass, calls the body a load one carries until it drops. விதியாம் எனச் சிலர் நோவது treats the mourners' appeal to fate as the wrong response; the right one is to have praised the feet beforehand.

818.reading: The poet sets two lives side by side. One man says 'we have prospered', helps none below him, pities his own life and no other, covets whatever he sees for the sake of food and tells the cooks what flavours he wants, eats and fills the pit that cannot be filled, orders about elders who outdo him in excellence, lineage, conduct and learning as if they were boys, tells lies and meanness to his base fellows and drops truth, honour and nobility; trusting himself, he leaves the good wife the ancients gave him, who would die at his death, and keeps a kept woman who craves food; clinging like oil to sesame to women who sell pleasure by the measure of money, hearing of chaste women in other men's houses he looks for the way in and not the fault; to the needy who come showing their skills he smiles and speaks sweetly as if about to give and gives nothing, wastes their days and the strength of their feet, scorns kin, says there is no here and no hereafter, lives without fear, practises deceit, desires wealth that is lightning, and thinks himself someone. The other life is that of your servants in Marudur, where the Kaveri's fish fight and swans sit on lotus leaves: they hold your feet, drop fear, do not count children, wife, kin and fortune as substance, think of your grace, push away Indra's wealth and the eight siddhis whenever they come, wear a rag and a loincloth, eat standing from a broken pot when someone gives, sleep on bare ground, embrace the woman called unfailing fitness and look on all lives as their children. Set side by side, the two are a hoof-print puddle and the deluge sea: alike as things, unlike in power; so I will put on service to the servants of your servants, grow used to them over long days, live beside them in this stout body, and take their feet's command on my head; if I see what I have seen, is there anything else good; nothing else is mine.
818.nuance: The householder is condemned not for having a house but for greed, contempt, lies and faithlessness; the servants' poverty is described as chosen (இந்திரச் செல்வமும் எட்டுச் சித்தியும் வந்துழி வந்துழி மறுத்தனர், refusing Indra's wealth and the eight siddhis whenever they come). ஓவாத் தகவு எனும் அரிவையைத் தழீஇ makes their only wife an abstraction, fitness or grace. The end is the poet's resolve to serve the servants' servants, the stance of 833 and 843.

819.reading: I have parted from hell; I have learned the way not to be born; I have escaped the dense arrows of Kama and his fighting round bow, having come inside the circle of Marudur of the Ancient One.
819.nuance: மருதவட்டம், the circle or precinct of Marudur, is set against Kama's வட்ட வில், the round bow, so the place itself is the shield. The verse is one of the few in the work where the poet speaks of the escape as already made.

820.reading: Heart, see: when you see the devotees, bow; think unforgettingly of Hara's red-gold anklet feet; go and meet the great Marudur; if you do not, Yama's men will carry you off, push you, throw you into hell and trample you.
820.nuance: The three commands rise from the devotees to the feet to the place, and the threat is plain hell, with none of the yogic reading other Siddhars give Yama. The address to the heart (நெஞ்சே) recurs at 831 and 838.

821.reading: Are there firm gains without toil, or helplessness that does not come from failing to toil? So dig the stump of deceit root and all out of the field of the heart, clear it, lay out the bed called love, spread the manure called truth, plant the single seed of doubtless devotion, water it daily with the clear water of ardour, and fearing the five cattle that break in past every guard, go in and build the fence of peace; then the great sprout of knowledge rises, shows the tender shoot of compassion, the weeds of lust and anger are pulled, it grows straight, the hair bristles, tears bud, the fragrant flower opens and the rare fruit of the five letters appears, with poison throat, three eyes, eight shoulders, five bright faces, coral colour and white ash, sweeter than the six tastes, a joy to see, hear and think of; the ruby fruit of high Marudur ripens slowly into the hand, and our kind eat it and hold their heads high. Some do not come this way: they make the field of the mind a waste, let the forest of lust cover it where the hunters of the five senses rob, chase the mirage-chariot of pleasure that is never reached, the deer of untaught sense wanders, and when the seed of desire is dropped the great poison tree called 'I' shoots up, puts out branches of lies, spreads leaves of sin, buds cruelty, flowers harshness, hangs fruit of sorrow, ripens death and falls into the serpent's place: useless to themselves and others, they pass in the blink of an eye; such is their nature.
821.nuance: The allegory is worked out stage by stage on both sides, cultivation and neglect, and the two trees are the Lord (the five-letter fruit wearing his own iconography) and the ego (யான் எனப் பெயரிய நச்சு மாமரம், the poison tree named 'I'). The five cattle and the five hunters are the senses in both halves. நாகிடை வீழ்ந்து, falling among the serpent, probably means hell; a variant reading is not recorded.

822.reading: Shrinking at the sound of the waist-bells and folding its hood, the serpent goes softly as the Lord of Marudur goes begging alms, so that Kama's hand-arrow may enter the women of fine jewels: see.
822.nuance: Read as the Bhikshatana scene in which Siva begs in the forest and the sages' wives fall in love with him: ஐயம் புகுவது is going for alms, and the snake on his body quiets so as not to frighten the women. The syntax leaves open whose waist-bells sound and whether காண் addresses the heart or the reader. This is the kovai's first akam fragment.

823.reading: You see no goal; you do not learn the five letters so as to master them; you do not cherish temple service; you do not speak his praise out of longing; you do not wear rudraksha; you do not smear ash everywhere: idle ones, is it easy to reach the feet of the Lord of Marudur?
823.nuance: This is a positive programme of ordinary Saiva practice, letters, service, praise, beads and ash, from a poet otherwise read as a renouncer of forms; 825 and 830 keep the same list. It stands far from Sivavakkiyar's dismissal of the same things, though both call the body's end the reason.

824.reading: Is it the mass of coarse hair, or the stretch of skin the hair grows on, or the wound packed inside the skin, or the blood that wells in the wound, or the bones standing here and there between, or the stinking marrow that drips from the bones, or the slime that oozes within, or the orderly files of crawling worms, or the heap of excrement set in water, or the ropes of tied nerves, or the disease that never leaves the body: which of these is 'I', I do not know; I searched everywhere and found it nowhere. Then, Lord of Marudur who burnt the three cities with one mountain bow, made Kama fine dust with a glance, turned the fire-mouthed poison to nectar so the gods would not die, stood beyond the two who sought you, and scorched Death for the boy's sake, half-woman, lord of Ganga, Lord of the Kaveri-girt grove where nine gems shine without the sun: because your divine grace came into my hand, I tore the veil of maya and gained the pure eye of knowledge; and having gained it I saw your greatness, and seeing it I saw myself, and saw others, and saw myself in all your states; those who do not see you are the kind that do not see themselves.
824.nuance: The dissection is a search for the self, each part posed as a question (ஓ), and the answer is that the self is not found in the body but given by grace along with the sight of the Lord. The order of seeing matters: the Lord first, then oneself, then others, then oneself in all his states. The variant தெரியாது இன்ன (not discerning, this) for தெரிதரல் இன்ன does not change the sense.

825.reading: Without thinking the five letters, without offering a green leaf, without pouring water: who are we, that we say we will reach the golden feet of the Lord of Marudur who dwells in the hearts of those who think of him?
825.nuance: The minimal offerings of 812 (a green leaf) are here the minimum demanded: the venba rebukes those, the poet included, who expect the feet while doing nothing at all. யாராயோ, who are we, is a self-address.

826.reading: We now know how matters stand between us, and may we say it: the Lord of Marudur, who adorned kings with flowers like the swans of the Marudur grove and made them survive and set a mark on them, should not himself load a burden on those who are already failing.
826.nuance: The kings saved and marked are taken by tradition as the Pandya Varaguna, whose brahmin-killing left him in this temple (839 names வரகுண தேவர்); the text itself only says he made kings survive and put a dot (பொட்டு) on them. The last line is clearer: it is not fitting to add a burden to one who is sinking, that is, to the poet. இடையுள்ள ஆறு may also pun on இடைமருது.

827.reading: After a long address, to the king who bent the mountain into a bow so the cities of his enemies burned in fire, white with fine ash, whose strong foot walked Kailasa, with the red-eyed bull of two horns like crescents, husband of the Himalaya's daughter, of Uma whose womb bore the seven worlds, father of the eight-shouldered elephant-eared boy and of Murugan of the cockerel banner and the hill-piercing spear, the poet asks whether the fault is yours: the sinners who do not think of you, do not clear away their crores of troubles, kill angry Death, scorn death and birth and wander like the calf of the gods' cow, the sin is theirs. If a man starves in front of a six-flavoured dish of rice with ghee and three fruits, it is not the food's fault; if he thirsts beside clear water cooled in the sun, it is not the water's fault; if he stands sweating in the open sun beside a grove dripping honey on cool sand, it is not the shade's fault.
827.nuance: The three comparisons make grace a thing set ready and unused, so the whole burden of failure falls on the one who does not come to it; the verse thereby denies that the Lord withholds. தேவர் ஆவின் கன்று, the calf of the heavenly cow, is the image for the freed one roaming at ease.

828.reading: Though the six faiths say 'no' and 'yes' and contradict one another, it all comes round to the Lord of Marudur, who dwells in the hearts of those who ever look to the One alone.
828.nuance: The verse does not refute the six; it lets them argue and says the end of every argument is the one Lord within. ஒருதனையே நோக்குவார் can be those who look to the one God or those who look at one thing with single mind; both suit.

829.reading: The merit of the Lord of the Kaveri-girt Marudur: his look made Kama's body dust; his toe pressed the rakshasa head downward; his sword-form rolled Daksha's head; and he sent Jalandhara's life away.
829.nuance: Four of the Lord's punitive deeds hang on one verb each (நோக்கிற்று, தாக்கிற்று, ஓக்கிற்று, போக்கிற்று), and the subject of all four is புண்ணியம், merit, so the deeds are the place's merit rather than the god's violence. The rakshasa is Ravana and the sword-form the discus given to Vishnu, as tradition has it.

830.reading: The poet addresses the Lord of Marudur who protects from entering the womb those devotees who worship with devotion grown to true love and offer a green leaf, nochi or karanthai. Many people leave children, wife, kin and house, go into forest and mountain, stand in summer in the midst of the five fires with arms raised and one leg bent, in rain and dew lie long in water, wear matted hair or pluck out their hair, go without eating, eat fruits, roots and wind-fallen leaves, air and water, sleep on salt ground and stones, and weaken the weakening body, tormenting themselves greatly for the sake of the Mother's release. We did none of this: in flawless seven-storied mansions, in red-pollen groves, breezy courtyards, painted halls, by lotus tanks and on peacock hills, wherever we wished, on ivory lion-legged cots with five-fold mattresses, white sheets smelling of flowers, cotton in silk, pillows, anklets sounding on the sheet, we embraced soft-spoken women with swan gait, waist-chains, snake-waists, swelling breasts, areca-smooth necks, bangled arms, ears, pearl-studded noses and eyes that carry Death's spear, Kama's arrow and the poison of the sea in moon faces under fresh garlands; we ate six-flavoured rice from gold plates, gave without limit to dancers, singers and the weary, anointed, adorned and garlanded ourselves, filled the five senses and rejoiced with sons and kin. Though we lived like this, because we kept the five letters of the mantra in the mouth unforgotten and sent the mind along your way, we have not lost that release; is this not your greatness? Whether a strong man throws it hard or a weak man throws it idly, the stone does not miss the ground: so those who utter your name do not fall from the good.
830.nuance: The verse ranks neither life; it makes the ascetic's self-torment and the poet's luxury equally irrelevant and the name and the directed mind the only cause of release. யாங்கள் (we) sets the poet, in tradition a merchant prince before his renunciation, among the pleasure-livers, which fits the legend but is also a rhetorical pose. The closing stone (கல்லே போல் நிலத்தின் வழாஅ) says the result does not depend on the thrower's strength.

831.reading: Heart, utter the name; can you waste away sinking into women's shoulders and talking lust? Encircle the Lord of the Marudur grove who wears the hide of the elephant he fought.
831.nuance: நாம நவிற்றாய் picks up the last word of 830 (நாமம் நவின்றோர்) and turns its general claim into an order to the heart. வளைந்து, encircle, is the word for going round the shrine as much as for clinging.

832.reading: Those who have reached the feet of the devotees of the Lord of Marudur with his golden konrai garland do not suffer hunger, do not grieve in disease, do not waste under Kama's arrow, do not stand yearning at the sight of wealth, and are not bound in this birth to enter the mire of hell: what do they owe to anyone?
832.nuance: The protection is given to those at the devotees' feet, one step further from the Lord than 820's devotees; 818 and 833 make the same descent, servant of the servants' servants. என் கடவார் (what do they owe) treats hunger, disease, lust and hell as debts the others still carry.

833.reading: After praising the Lord of Marudur who gives unending joy and undiminishing wealth to those who reach his feet, who has no root, middle or end and is beyond the three times, hidden from the eye of flesh and not from the mind's eye, the unflickering light, the sound that rises from within and does not reach the ear's hole, the divine honey that wells sweetly inside past the tongue, the fragrance of knowledge that comes by no nostril, who is himself all things, in whom all appearing appears while he appears in nothing else, with the white moon on his spread hair and the dark throat, whom Vishnu, Brahma and the Vedas still pursue, the ruby of Marudur with three unwinking eyes, the poet asks him to hear a servant's plea without anger. Dragged by the cruel deeds of long consorting with hard-hearted base men who do not bow to your feet, I lay long in the dark prison-cell called the womb, chained with the chain of the gut, like a caged worm sunk in long filth, suffering, rained on by many diseases, pressed by the punishers, writhing in the belly's fire, beaten by the whip of wind, unable to lie, stand or walk, cramped in the narrow gate; then, placed in the portion of sin, with the five cruel guards set over me, tied in the long rope of desire, I and the body were bound in bonds and let softly out. I too went and roamed in evil, wronged the great, seized others' goods, failed in pity, killed many lives, praised the look of other men's wives, told many lies, kept base company and fed the craving of the five, gathered what I gathered and came back, did not give where giving was due nor fall where falling was due, and now I have met trouble and lie withering for many days and see no road to release. Count me too a slave to the servants of the servants who reached you, with the green leaf I offered make me know, free me from this prison, guard me from entering the prison again, O one with red hair like gathered fire.
833.nuance: The womb passage inverts 808: the same ten months told from inside as a cell, with the umbilical cord as chain (குடர் என் சங்கிலி), the five senses as the warders appointed at birth (காவல் கொடியோர் ஐவர்), and desire as the rope that binds soul and body together in பாசம். தண்டனாளர், the punishers, and வாத மத்திகை, the whip of wind, are unexplained; the latter may be the womb's wind humour. The variant தத்துவ for தற்பர (833 line 14) would make the Lord the tattva rather than the Supreme.

834.reading: One woman is settled on his matted hair and another shines on the side of his body; if the bull has gone and this girl gives the Lord of Marudur her conch bangles and her garment, where is she to be?
834.nuance: An akam fragment: the girl wasting for love of the Lord loses her bangles and her waist's slenderness (the stock signs of மெலிவு), figured as giving them to him, and her companion asks where she can stand when Ganga has the hair and Uma the body. சங்கே கலையே can be conch-bangles and cloth or, in the cipher of love poetry, the slipping bangles and the waist; விடையே போய் is obscure, perhaps 'the bull having gone (as his messenger)'. The variant இடைப்புகு (entering the waist) suggests another reading of the last line.

835.reading: Within Marudur the gods and the four Vedas crowd and press; going into its long interior in that press they cannot come back out; cutting away crookedness and the harm of the five, he is the bright light that sprouts within the one-pointed gathering of a mind made straight.
835.nuance: The gods and Vedas that crowd into the shrine do not find their way out, while the light appears in the single-pointed mind: the verse sets the inner finding above the outer press without rejecting the shrine. ஒருக்கும் ஒருக்கத்தின் உள்ளே, within the one-making of the one-pointed, is the yogic word for concentration.

836.reading: Saying 'you hold the blazing trident', 'you rode the bull', 'you ate the poison none can eat', 'you burnt Kama with your eye', 'you burnt the three cities', 'you wore the elephant's hide', 'you wore the serpent', 'you hold fire in your hand', 'you killed Death', 'you cut Jalandhara's body', 'you trod the boastful rakshasa', 'you broke Daksha's sacrifice', 'you wore the fierce tiger skin', 'you grew till the sky was below you and the boar and the swan could not reach', 'you crushed the fire-eyed dwarf who ate the lives of the earth': praising your countless unimaginable fame is only as far as my trembling mind's words go; your measureless greatness is beyond my measure, but with poor words that do not fit I look to you, so do not fail to clear my troubles and leave me in distress, O rich light seated in Marudur where cloth banners wake the clouds asleep on the seven-storied mansions, wonder-dancer who pours grace: even for the wicked Buddhist who threw a stone at you, because he threw it thinking of you, grace did not fail.
836.nuance: The list of deeds is framed as inadequate speech (புன்மொழி) offered anyway, and its proof is Sakkiya Nayanar, who in the Periyapuranam worshipped by throwing a stone daily: the act was accepted because of the thought behind it (நின் நினைந்து எறிந்த அதனால்). This makes intention, not form, the condition of grace, as 830 and 848 do.

links.note: Both of Pattinathar's agavals make a green leaf enough: the Kachchi agaval says he pities devotees who offer even a green leaf and grants the house of Siva's state; the Marudur opening says he gives release even to devotees who offer a green leaf. The Kazhumalam kovai (853) reduces even that to the heart.

Sivavakkiyar tells the builders of houses and performers of sacrifice that when the Arbiter's summons comes the body will not fetch a potsherd's price; Pattinathar says the bundle of the carcass falls and goes and the mourners call it fate. Both make the body's certain drop the reason to turn now, Sivavakkiyar to the inner Lord, Pattinathar to the praised feet.

Tirumular promises the worshipper of the chakra Indra's wealth first, then the eight siddhis, and release last; Pattinathar's servants push away Indra's wealth and the eight siddhis whenever they arrive and keep only the feet. The same sequence is offered in one text and declined in the other, so Pattinathar qualifies the gifts as things a devotee refuses rather than denying that they come.

Tirumular says the Lord stays in a heart tilled like a field for those who can praise him there; Pattinathar works the figure out stage by stage, stump of deceit dug out, bed of love, manure of truth, seed of devotion, water of ardour, fence of peace, until the Lord himself is the ripe fruit in the hand.

Tirumular's deeds depart like strong weeds when the Lord takes his place in a mind polished to a jewel; Pattinathar's farmer pulls the weeds of lust and anger so that the sprout of knowledge grows straight. In both the weeds are what the mind grows of itself and the Lord's presence is what clears them.

The Kural's rule for a real field, manuring before ploughing and guarding after weeding, is the order Pattinathar's heart-farmer follows: he manures with truth before sowing and builds the fence of peace against the five cattle after pulling the weeds. The farming knowledge is the same; Pattinathar moves it to the mind.

Both venba-side verses give the same minimum programme as the condition of the feet: five letters, service or offerings, praise, beads and ash in 823; five letters, a green leaf and water in 825. 823 rebukes the idle, 825 includes the poet among them.

The Naladiyar's fool calls a pot that seeps filth from nine openings 'broad-shouldered one' because the dark skin dazzles him; Pattinathar lifts the skin and lists what is under it, hair, wound, blood, bone, marrow, slime, worms, excrement, nerves and disease, and asks which of them is 'I'. The Naladiyar aims at desire, Pattinathar at the self.

In the Kachchi agaval Pattinathar takes the lover's praised body part by part, sole, calf, thigh, belly, breast, hand, neck, mouth, teeth, nose, eyes, ears and hair, and shows each as bone, slime, sweat or oozing; here he turns the same dissection on himself and makes it a search for the self, which neither body yields.

Tirumular says those who do not think of the Lord have no joy of him, like the kite perched in the palmyra beside its fruit; Pattinathar says the fault is not the Lord's but the sinners' who do not think of him, like a man starving before a dish or thirsting beside cool water. Both make the Lord's availability the measure of the unthinking one's loss.

Tirumular says those who saw the six sects did not see him, since he is not what the six hold; Pattinathar lets the six contradict one another and says all of it comes round to the Lord in the hearts of those who look to the One. Both deny the sects a hold on him, but Pattinathar grants that their quarrel arrives at him in the end.

Arunagirinathar says 'enough' to hearing the six faiths argue their many arts; Pattinathar says they say 'no' and 'yes' against one another and that none of it matters to the one who looks to the One. Both poets treat the sects' dispute as noise around a single object.

Tirumular says those who stay in the household are equal to great ascetics if they keep the Lord in thought; Pattinathar says that those who lived in mansions with women and gold plates lost no release because the five letters stayed in the mouth and the mind went the Lord's way. Tirumular states the equality, Pattinathar stages it against the five-fire ascetics.

Tirumular says that even making one's bones the firewood and frying one's flesh does not reach his gem without melting love; Pattinathar lists the five fires, the water, the plucked hair and the stone beds and says the self-tormentors gain nothing the name-sayer lacks. Both make the body's suffering no currency.

The Naladiyar ranks striving in austerity as the best way to live and dwelling with those one loves as the middle; Pattinathar says the austerities bring the ascetics no more than the man who dwelt with women and kin and kept the name on his lips. The conflict holds if the Naladiyar's ranking is of the paths to the goal; if it ranks only the dignity of lives, Pattinathar is answering a different question.

The Udarkootru Vannam tells the ten months from outside, seed and blood becoming organs and a form in which life grows; here the same months are told from inside as a dark cell with the gut for a chain, worms, disease, belly-fire and the whip of wind, and the birth as release into the custody of five guards. The two are one poet's two accounts of the same time.

812 ends by asking not to enter the prison of the womb (சிறைக் கருப்பாசயம்) again; 833 describes that prison cell by cell and ends with the same request, this prison escaped, not to enter the prison again.

Tirumular says that in the womb maya joins her brood to the soul, thought arises, karma takes hold and maya's bonds begin; Pattinathar is dragged into the womb by the deeds of bad company and comes out with the five guards set over him and desire's rope tying him to the body in bonds (பாசம்). Both locate the start of bondage in the womb and name the bonds.

Tirumular says the Lord is not in the mansion, hall, courtyard, temple or holy garb but in the hidden place in the heart of those who have given up longing; Pattinathar says the gods and Vedas crowd into the shrine of Marudur and do not come out, while the light sprouts inside the one-pointed mind. Both put the finding inside the person, not the building.

source_issues: The metre labels printed beside the ids (நேரிசையாசிரியப்பா / நேரிசைவெண்பா and so on) carry the previous unit's metre over to the next and do not describe the unit they stand beside; 816, 819, 822, 825, 828, 831 and 834 are venbas, 817, 820, 823, 826, 829, 832 and 835 kalitthurais.
813 ends without a final punctuation mark and 815 lines ராரணந் தொடராப் and வேண்டு் carry stray or missing characters (ஆரணம், வேண்டும்).
821 line 22 காள கண்டமுங் கண்ணொரு மூன்றுந்' has a stray apostrophe; line 24 தோ ளிருநான்குஞ் is split mid-word (தோளிருநான்கும்).
818 and 833 carry editor's variant notes numbered [5] to [8] and [17] to [19] whose anchors are not marked in the text.
822 and 824 are headed with the previous unit's metre as well as their own; see the general note.
